reviews.text: 10 hour refresh on the review: There's a shocking amount of depth as you keep getting further and further into the game. The amount of ways you can go about climbing the tower keeps increasing, and there's a ton of customization allowed. My number one recommendation: Don't let curses just sit, thinking they're only a challenge mode. Breaking into them completely changes the playstyle. Super fun game! Charming, good brain teaser, and cute graphics/sounds! Easy recommendation, especially at that price point!

Updated review: I'm changing my opinion. As I've gotten further into the game I've run into more no-win situations, some of which appear to be by-design. The one that just made me change my review and uninstall was one where I was a broken pot away from unlocking two new characters on the same run (321 coins and buy all shop items) and I got cornered by a ghost enemy, which cannot be killed with the starter weapon, only knocked back. One too many kicks-in-the-sack, and I'm out. Sorry. It's cute. It feels like it should be fun. But, in the end, it's a game designed for masochists, and I have a limited supply of frustration in any given day and don't want to burn it here. If you like beat-your-head-against-the-wall-until-you-finally-win kinds of games (you know who you are) then you'll probably like this. Not for me. Original review: This is a tentative upvote. The game is quite cute. It is also BRUTALLY unforgiving. It's not unfair -- all the information is right there on the screen for you to see and the enemies appear to behave deterministically -- but if you misjudge something you can die in just a couple of moves. This is especially true as you go up the tower and enemy patterns increase in movement complexity, health, damage, and even kill-condition (some need to be knocked into a pit). When you die it's your fault, but it sometimes it feels like it comes out of nowhere (and other times you make a move and realize you just royally screwed yourself).

Really cool in theory but hard to recommend as-is. This is partially skill issue, but the visual clarity could really use some work. In games like Into the Breach, you know exactly how your movement is going to affect enemies on the next turn. In Bobo's Big Tower, you kind of just have to guess what's about to happen next. You get so many attack squares as you get deeper into your run, but it gets to the point where you're not sure if you're even going to move when you input a direction or if you're going to hit a random pot and stay still. It doesn't seem feasible to mentally calculate this every single input with no visual feedback. This is also true for enemies- I get that I'm going to take damage on this tile if I do nothing, but what if I knock an enemy back? Am I still taking damage? The answer is sometimes yes, sometimes no depending on the enemy and situation. It makes for a frustrating experience. Finally, it's really annoying to have to go through the first floor over and over and over just to die to something you've either never seen before, or again, due to some issue with visual clarity. Games like Spelunky let you start a run from whatever floor once you've unlocked them, and I really feel like this game could use a feature like that to let me practice later floors without having to run it back from zero just to have a chance of seeing them again. This game has potential, and some very simple QOL fixes could make it great, but I can't recommend it as-is

Bobo's big tower is a great pickup. The game has a simple premise, but it quickly grows in complexity as you venture higher into the tower. Getting a winning run requires you to REALLY TAKE YOUR TIME AND PLAN!! Getting some crazy items helps too :)

It's very mixed for me. There's quite a ton of strategy that goes into each move. But the unlock system and especially the weapon upgrades feel much more frustrating than fun. Rather than knowing how your going to move, especially with the large disjointed weapons you hit a pot or statue way off in the distance which leads to cornering and a swift death. Many of the non weapon upgrades seem fun and a way to help your way through the tower. If they even wish to show up in the pool at all. It could just be bad rng from how seeds go. But just the way enemies can combo you alongside killing you in just 1 hit makes it much more frustrating to lose off of 1 mistake especially with the time it takes to grind back up on the off chance you get an upgrade which helps more than harms. As for the good. The art style, the music, and the core gameplay style all is very fun and addictive. I just wish the additional weapons felt good to use rather than being disappointed if that's all a shop contains.

Some people will probably love this game but it just isn't for me. The combat is interesting, with little combos you can do if you position your character correctly (i especially liked the wind spell basically giving your default attack more range if you spin around), however for the most part I found that weapons were more of a hinderance than a help. I did not notice a damage increase from picking up multiple of one item (they just put an extra attack next to the already existing one, which i never found helpful) and the extra attacks from different weapons would make me accidentally hit objects and advance the turn order when I wanted to move instead (this especially applies to the fire spell which i don't think i found a good use case for ever). Of course the game is designed around not ending up in a situation where you might hit stuff but i found this basically impossible in most rooms if you have a few items equipped. An especially egregious example of this was when I was using an extra sword and then died instantly after entering a room because there was an explosive next to the door and I was forced to hit it as I walked in. Even when I had a bunch of different weapons swinging I never felt like I was getting any more powerful; the wind spell was the only time I felt like I really got an upgrade, otherwise I could have like 8 attack boxes on the screen and only feel like 2 or 3 of them were actually doing anything. Speaking of weapons, another thing I found strange was that despite using gems to unlock multiple new items, I only ever saw ~6 unique items throughout my 90 minutes of playing. A sword, daggers, a wind spell, a fire spell, a magnet and an item that full healed you. I don't know I just got unlucky or if this is intentional but either way it didn't feel good walking into the same shop run after run with the same expensive and generally not useful items. This is excluding the items I got to choose from the monster soul thingys shop, but those all seemed rare and even more useless than the normal shop items, one doing literally nothing and others exchanging health for something. With how limited your health is these did not seem great. Speaking of health, this game is absolutely brutal. Amazing for some I'm sure but not for me. With 4 hp a single mistake or miscalculation can easily lead to you losing most of your health. If you aren't thinking about literally every step you can easily get put into forced damage situations against even the most common enemy. Rooms on the third floor and above with multiple enemies started to feel like games of chess, figuring out how each enemy is going to move and where your attacks are going to rotate to. I'm sure this strategic play sounds like im actually writing a positive review for some, but well... i've never been very good at chess :P. The harsh penalty for taking damage is made even more difficult given that hearts are an rng drop and you can easily go multiple rooms without getting one, let alone 3 for a full heal. I'm sure there are items to increase your max health but as I said I never saw any. My problem with this game isn't that it was frustrating, i just wasn't really having fun. It felt like I had clocked into my shift at the pot breaking factory to earn gold at a slow rate only to spend it on items that hindered me more than they helped me. The combat past the first floor was more interesting, with weapon combos being used against actually interesting enemy ai, but the default enemy set just seemed very strange to me. The slimes and spiders simply keel over and die but the skeletons are either the easiest thing ever at certain distances, but at other distances (or when there's multiple) you'll be being chased around in circles or backed into a corner and forced to take damage. I know the whole point of the game is using the environment to advance the turn order, but sometimes there just isn't a pot to run to and the way to avoid damage was take a different route through the room 20 turns ago, or your extra weapons have destroyed all the terrain while you were walking and now there's nothing left. The items i used mostly felt detrimental to my build (except wind spell i love you wind spell) and i never felt like i was getting any stronger despite making it a few floors up. I would definitely give this game a try if you're a roguelike fan who also enjoys chess and other similar activities that require the use of ones brain but as someone who doesn't enjoy monotonous gameplay (don't check my rain world hours) and is maybe a tad dense unfortunately this one is not for me

It's a 4/10 turn-based puzzle roguelight with some slight Binding of Issac feel to it (gameplay not atmosphere). +Novel gameplay. +Short runs 1-10 min usually (it's very quick and easy just to jump into another run). =Graphics and Sound are slightly below par for this type of game, but just just slightly. -UI You don't know what your starting items do due to lack of tooltips (only way to find out is by playing). --Progression, the move stuff you unlock and the better you get at the game the less of the items you actually want to have in your item pool as it just make the game harder (negative progression is never a good feeling, then I finally beat the game I locked down everything 'cept the starting sword and gust magic for consistent shops).

[SUMMARY] The Labyrinths of Legend of Zelda (1986) and Lights Out Cube (1995) chess style puzzle game comingled to test your skills and patience. This atmospheric retro game has a quick learning curve, but knowing the move set doesn't make it any easier (like Chess). Each room is randomized and requires you to preplan your next 2-3 steps to ensure a proper setup to kill the various enemies, however you can pick a seed number (like perhaps 666) to re-playthrough the exact labyrinth layout if you are trying to best a specific walkthrough. The base enemy (skeleton) attacks straight on and requires two hits, so either you need to ensure he has a buffer space behind him or already have one hit in before striking him with a wall behind him. The various treasure pots are used strategically to be struck so as to pass a movement turn, whereas the enemies are always forced to move once towards you every single time (the game performs a back and forth round based system like cards or chess). Some enemies, like bats, can only attack on the diagonal or only move once every two turns. The more enemies and barrels you kill/destroy the more coins you can collect which can be used for health restore or weapon upgrades. Weapon upgrades will allow your hit zones to expand to multiple boxes, which when used properly can be a great advantage. You will need to be aware of the flammable bomb barrels, however the game pre-notifies you whether or not moving into a square is dangerous move or not. The 8-bit atmospheric retro music compliments the game well and reminds me of a game like Inscryption. [SUGGESTIONS] 1) I feel like the game would benefit from a limited use "Restart Room" option. Once you start to progress far into the game you make a mistake move in a room and realize you're checkmated it can be frustrating to have to start all over again. Even if its once per playthrough that still would be a sweet addition. 2) A little more explanation on the Secrets+ would help. As you progress you find "Secrets" which seem like they more like boosters/stat enhancers. 3) Unless I am missing something you can't go back upstairs once you go down. I wanted to return to a upgrade dealer as I few a few coins short and realized I couldn't go back up which seemed odd. [RATING] 8/10 [FINAL THOUGHTS] As a kid who grew up playing puzzle games, specifically lights out cube, this game is both challenging, fun and frustrating. Its the perfect way to take your mind off of the world around you and focus in on something that stimulates your mind in a good way. Shout out to the dev and GrandPooBear and his team for the great addition to my steam library // xoxo MariosDumper //

It feels bad, but I have to give this game a negative review. It does a lot well, but has some major problems which just make it far too punishing. I love the graphics, the music and sound design are great too. The game is a rogue-like, which I normally love, but I just can't with this game. It is extremely easy to die in this game, and to the games credit it's really quick to start up a new run. However it starts to become frustrating when you start getting locked in rooms with literally no way to succeed. The in game economy doesn't feel balanced either, most items have very high costs and aren't very useful. Some of the time you'll clear the entire floor and not even have enough currency for a single upgrade. Upgrades in the game come in the form of weapons and spells, all of which add more tiles to your attack. This also comes with a negative however, because that also changes if you will move or attack by accident and end up taking damage instead. You unlock new potential upgrades by completing in game challenges, however you then also need to buy the unlock with Gems, another currency you can rarely find in game. This feels like an unnecessary extra hurdle, as you can end up completing a challenge only to have no Gems to actually get your new gear. The game also doesn't really give you any help at all. Some of the enemies on later floors just don't die, with the game giving you no feedback as to why. At one point I hit some creature at least 7 times in a row, to seemingly no effect, only to have it kill me in one hit when I tried to move around it to maybe hit it from another side. I'm not sure how long the game is, as I've never managed to complete a single run successfully in all my time playing. I've never seen the titular Bobo, so I'm not sure how far along in the game I was.

Brushing past the "Issac + Necrodancer" framing, Bobo's uniqueness come from your adorable character bouncing around, gathering power they can't control, and dying from it. Every weapon added to your person requires a little more tactical forethought as you can accidently screw yourself with your expanding range of attack and hubris. Creating a odd depth and nice mix with the kiddy retro theme that keeps the game fun even as you make forced errors and imperfections. Very worth the price, Recommended for all "Just a little guy" enjoyers

Developed by SillyKitty and published by DarkBear Studios, Bobo's Big Tower is a delightful indie roguelike that embraces a retro identity while delivering surprisingly deep gameplay systems. Built around the visual language of classic handheld games, it immediately captures attention with its Game Boy Color-inspired presentation, featuring vibrant pixel art and a playful fantasy setting. Rather than simply relying on nostalgia, the game uses its old-school appearance as a framework for a thoughtful adventure centered on strategy, exploration, and experimentation. The premise is simple but entertaining: the villainous necromancer Bobo has begun constructing a gigantic tower reaching toward Heaven in an attempt to harness unimaginable power, and a group of heroes must climb its floors to prevent disaster from engulfing the realm. The tower itself serves as the game's greatest strength. Every floor is procedurally generated, ensuring that no two ascents feel exactly alike. Players must search for keys, navigate hazards, and contend with a variety of enemies while carefully considering every movement they make. Unlike action-heavy roguelikes that reward quick reactions, Bobo's Big Tower operates on a turn-based movement system where enemies act only after the player moves. This mechanic transforms each encounter into a tactical puzzle, encouraging patience and planning. Even a single misplaced step can create complications, making victories feel earned rather than accidental. The result is a gameplay loop that is easy to understand but difficult to master. Progression remains engaging thanks to the game's diverse roster of playable characters. While Bibi serves as the starting hero, additional adventurers become available over time, each offering their own combat style, equipment preferences, and pieces of lore. These differing perspectives provide strong incentives for repeated playthroughs, as players not only experiment with new strategies but also uncover more information about the world and its eccentric inhabitants. The narrative isn't presented through lengthy exposition; instead, it unfolds gradually through repeated runs, giving the game an appealing sense of mystery that complements its roguelike structure. Equipment and customization are another highlight. Weapons come in many forms, from traditional melee options to magical and ranged alternatives, while artifacts introduce modifiers that can dramatically change a run's trajectory. Some items provide obvious advantages, whereas others present unusual trade-offs that require players to adapt their approach. This willingness to let experimentation drive the experience keeps the gameplay fresh across multiple sessions. Optional curses and challenge modifiers further expand replayability, offering veterans additional ways to test their understanding of the mechanics. It is the kind of design that rewards curiosity, making every discovery feel meaningful. Presentation is consistently charming throughout. The limited color palette and expressive pixel work successfully recreate the atmosphere of late-1990s handheld gaming without feeling restrictive. Character designs are memorable, environments remain easy to read during gameplay, and the soundtrack by Mysty McAllister adds a fitting sense of adventure and whimsy. Together, the visuals and audio establish a personality that separates Bobo's Big Tower from many contemporary indie releases. It manages to feel both nostalgic and modern, paying tribute to its influences while confidently standing on its own. That said, the game may not appeal equally to everyone. Players expecting fast-paced combat could find its deliberate pace somewhat slow, and the randomness inherent to roguelikes occasionally results in runs that feel more difficult than others. Certain character unlocks also introduce a steeper challenge curve that may discourage less patient players. However, these drawbacks are relatively minor when weighed against the game's creativity, replay value, and polished execution. Bobo's Big Tower succeeds because it understands the appeal of classic game design while enhancing it with contemporary roguelike ideas. Its combination of tactical movement, procedural exploration, character variety, and retro charm creates an experience that is both accessible and rewarding. For fans of strategy-focused indie titles, it offers many hours of engaging experimentation and discovery wrapped in an irresistibly charming package. Rating: 7/10
